title: Subtour-LP integrality gap for metric TSP
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal: Determine \(\Gamma =\sup _{n\ge 3,c} \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}(c)/\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}(c)\), where c ranges over every metric on n labeled points and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\) is the symmetric subtour relaxation defined below.
definitions: For \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and \(E=\{\{u,v\}:u\ne v\}, a\) metric has \(c_{uu}=0, c_{uv}=c_{vu}>0\) for \(u\ne v\), and \(c_{uv}\le c_{uw}+c_{wv}\). Costs are arbitrary real numbers; no Euclidean embedding is assumed. \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\) is the minimum sum of edge costs on a Hamiltonian cycle of the complete undirected graph. For \(S\subseteq V, \delta (S)\) contains edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and \(x(F)=\sum_{e\in F}x_{e}\). Define \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}=\min  \sum_{e} c_{e} x_{e}\) subject to \(x(\delta (\{v\}))=2\) for every \(v, x(\delta (S))\ge 2\) for every nonempty proper \(S\subsetneq V\), and \(0\le x_{e}\le 1\) for every e. The LP is feasible and has positive optimum. The supremum ranges over every finite size, not one fixed n. This is the symmetric metric subtour-LP integrality gap, not an approximation ratio measured only against \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\), an asymmetric TSP relaxation, or a restricted geometric metric.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \Gamma |\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.
why: The exact strength of the principal relaxation for a canonical optimization problem, joining polyhedral structure, probabilistic rounding and approximation. A resolution would explain a longstanding gap between fractional connectivity and integral tours.

importance.reason: A defining integrality-gap conjecture in combinatorial optimization with consequences for LP rounding and the limits of metric TSP approximation methods.

progress.text: Wolsey’s LP-relative analysis gives the classical upper bound \(3/2\), as recalled in the inherited reference.
Karlin–Klein–Oveis Gharan prove the general LP integrality gap is at most \(3/2- \varepsilon\) for an absolute \(\varepsilon >10^{- 36}\).
Gurvits–Klein–Leake improve the explicit LP-relative saving to \(2.18\cdot 10^{- 34}\); Lemma 4.5 supplies the relevant denominator.
Jin–Klein–Williamson’s journal article proves \(4/3\) for the half-integral cycle-cut class; its preprint first appeared in 2022.
Villa–Vercesi–Barta–Mastrolilli revise the theorem for optimal LP solutions with at most \(n+6\) nonzero coordinates.
The inherited revised paper gives a \(10/7\) guarantee for the maximum-entropy algorithm on a class whose gap is already at most \(4/3\).
Song claims an LP-relative saving exceeding \(2.05522\cdot 10^{- 30}\); recorded as a fresh unverified preprint claim, not a resolution.
Cook–Hougardy–Petrich extend their reported exact verification to \(n=16\) generally and \(n=18\) for half-integral extreme points.

references.title: A Sharper Explicit Bound on the Subtour-LP Integrality Gap for Metric TSP

status_note: The general \(4/3\) equality remains open through the primary-source review of 11 September 2026. The established explicit upper bound recorded here is \(3/2- 2.18\cdot 10^{- 34}; a\) September 2 preprint claims a further small improvement, clearly separated from verified literature. Restricted-class theorems and finite-size verification do not resolve the universal conjecture. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.

context_blocks.text: The target is the value of the universal integrality gap. The classical \(4/3\) conjecture proposes \(\Gamma =4/3; a\) larger determined value is also an answer to this quantitative question.

The relaxation allows fractional edge purchases while retaining two elementary properties of every tour: each vertex has degree two, and every nontrivial cut is crossed at least twice. It therefore knows much more than a disconnected cycle-cover relaxation, but its feasible points need not be convex combinations of Hamiltonian cycles. The conjecture asks for the exact worst loss caused by that remaining freedom.

For example, a feasible fractional vector may put positive weight on several alternative connections at one vertex without choosing a single predecessor and successor. The cut inequalities ensure aggregate connectivity, yet they do not force these local choices to assemble into one integral cycle. The proposed factor \(4/3\) says that, in a metric, repairing all such inconsistencies never costs more than one third of the fractional optimum.

The metric assumption is what makes shortcutting possible. If a connected Eulerian multigraph visits a vertex several times, replacing a detour by the direct edge between its endpoints does not increase cost. One can consequently search for a suitably cheap Eulerian structure rather than construct a Hamiltonian cycle at every intermediate step. This observation explains why spanning trees and parity correction recur in approximation algorithms for the problem.

A minimum spanning tree followed by a minimum-cost matching on its odd-degree vertices yields the classical \(3/2\) guarantee. Wolsey’s analysis measures both components against the LP: the tree costs at most the fractional optimum, and the matching at most half that value. The inherited July 2026 paper recalls this argument before studying a particular randomized refinement.

An algorithmic ratio and an integrality-gap ratio must use the correct denominator. A guarantee cost\(\le \alpha \cdot \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\) does not establish \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}\le \alpha \cdot \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\), since the fractional optimum can be smaller. Karlin–Klein–Oveis Gharan’s FOCS 2022 result explicitly supplies an LP-relative guarantee below \(3/2\), extending the earlier approximation breakthrough. It is this later theorem that directly improves the general gap bound.

The modern approach samples a spanning tree from a distribution constrained by fractional edge marginals, then corrects its parity. Tree cost and parity-repair cost interact, so treating the two separately can lose the desired saving. Gurvits–Klein–Leake strengthen probability estimates using capacities of real stable polynomials. Their Lemma 4.5 is explicitly LP-relative and yields the certified bound \(\Gamma \le 3/2- 2.18\cdot 10^{- 34}\). The small constant reflects a worst-case proof, not a claim that practical tours are that close to \(3/2\).

A class can have a better integrality gap than the worst ratio of a particular algorithm on it. Jin–Klein–Williamson prove the \(4/3\) bound for half-integral cycle-cut instances using a specialized construction. Half-integral means that nonzero fractional coordinates are \(1/2\) or 1, with an additional restriction on the hierarchy of tight cuts. This result does not cover every half-integral instance, still less every subtour solution.

Their July 2026 paper, which supplied the inherited reference, proves a \(10/7\) guarantee for the maximum-entropy algorithm on that same restricted class. Since \(10/7\) exceeds \(4/3\), it improves understanding of the chosen algorithm rather than improving the already-known class gap. The authors also identify examples giving a lower bound of \(11/8\) on the algorithm’s performance. Such an algorithm-specific obstruction cannot refute the conjecture about the cheapest possible tour.

Two complementary approaches restrict the fractional solution in other ways. Villa–Vercesi–Barta–Mastrolilli prove the \(4/3\) bound when an optimal solution has at most \(n+6\) nonzero components, combining structural reasoning and computation. This is a support-size condition, not a theorem for every instance on at most \(n+6\) vertices. Larger support remains outside its stated guarantee.

Cook–Hougardy–Petrich’s September 8, 2026 revision reports exact verification for all metric instances through \(n=16\) and for half-integral extreme points through \(n=18\). It also repairs omissions in earlier extreme-point lists. This is stronger evidence than sampling finitely many random metrics, because the computation organizes the relevant polyhedral cases. It still leaves unbounded n, and the catalogue has not rerun that enumeration.

A September 2 preprint by Zhao Song claims a larger universal saving, \(\varepsilon\)★>\(2.05522\cdot 10^{- 30}\), through a refined maximum-entropy analysis. Its main theorem is explicitly relative to \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\). The statement was checked, but the lengthy proof and numerical certificate were not independently verified here, so the value is recorded as a recent claim rather than silently replacing the established bound. Even if confirmed, it would remain far above the conjectured ratio \(4/3\).

sentences: The metric traveling-salesperson problem asks for a cheapest tour through every point.
Its subtour linear program permits fractional edges while preserving degree and cut constraints.
This card asks for the supremum ratio of the integral tour optimum to that relaxation over all finite metrics.
The classical \(4/3\) conjecture identifies a proposed value of this ratio.
Benchmark acceptance requires a Lean-certified numerical value within absolute error 0.01, without assuming the supremum is attained.
